title: Torrone morbido
subtitle: soft Italian nougat with honey, almonds, and toasted pistachios
excerpt: Torrone morbido is the soft, yielding Italian nougat made for Christmas, as opposed to the hard, crunchy version (torrone duro). It is made by cooking honey and sugar to separate temperatures, combining them with beaten egg whites into a thick, silky Italian meringue, then folding in toasted nuts. The result is ivory-white, slightly chewy, and intensely sweet; best cut into small pieces and eaten at room temperature.
sourceNotes: Torrone is an Italian confection with roots in the Arab sugar-and-honey nougat tradition introduced to southern Europe via Sicily. The soft version, torrone morbido, is associated with Cremona in Lombardy (where the confection has been made since at least the 15th century) and is eaten throughout Italy at Christmas. Pellegrino Artusi documented a recipe for Torrone in La Scienza in Cucina (1891). The method here follows the traditional two-temperature technique: honey and sugar are cooked separately then combined with Italian meringue.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze wrapped tightly in baking paper then cling film. Defrost at room temperature for 1 hour.
recipe.batchNotes: The method requires attention at two simultaneous temperatures; larger batches are not practical without two thermometers and two pans.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keep wrapped in baking paper in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 2 weeks.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cooked meringue made by pouring hot sugar syrup (at hard-ball stage, around 121°C) into beaten egg whites while the mixer runs. The heat pasteurises the whites and produces a stable, dense, glossy meringue used in nougat, buttercream, and soufflé glacé.

content.text: Torrone morbido requires cooking two things at once: honey to 130°C in one pan and a sugar syrup to hard-ball stage (121°C) in another, then pouring both into beaten egg whites in sequence to build an

base. A stand mixer is needed to keep the whites beating while you pour. This is an advanced recipe, not because any single step is complicated, but because accurate temperature control of two pans simultaneously is required. Line your tin before you start; once the nougat is ready it sets quickly.
Prepare the tin and toast the nuts

Line a 20 cm square tin with a sheet of baking paper on the base and sides, leaving enough overhang to fold over the top. Lightly oil the paper. Spread {{almonds}} and {{pistachios}} on a baking tray and toast at 160°C for 8 minutes until lightly coloured. Transfer to a bowl and keep warm; cold nuts seize the nougat as it is poured.

Put {{honey}} in a small heavy-based saucepan over a medium heat. Clip a thermometer to the pan. In a separate pan, combine {{caster-sugar}} and {{water}} and stir to dissolve over a medium heat. Once dissolved, stop stirring and bring to hard-ball stage, 121°C. At the same time, bring the honey to 130°C. Both will need to reach their temperatures at roughly the same time. Start the honey about 5 minutes after the sugar.

While the sugars cook, whisk {{egg-whites}} in a stand mixer on high speed until they hold stiff peaks. When the honey reaches 130°C, reduce the mixer to medium speed and pour the hot honey in a thin, steady stream down the inside of the bowl, avoiding the whisk. Increase speed to high and whisk for 1 minute. Then, with the mixer still running, pour the sugar syrup in the same way. Whisk on high speed for 5 minutes until the meringue is thick, glossy, and barely warm. Add {{vanilla-extract}} and {{sea-salt-fine}} and mix briefly.
Fold in the nuts and set

Switch to a spatula and fold the warm nuts quickly into the nougat base. The mixture will be extremely thick and sticky. Scrape immediately into the lined tin and press level with oiled hands or an oiled spatula. Fold the baking paper over the top and press a second tin or a board on top to flatten. Leave at room temperature for at least 4 hours, or overnight, until firm. Cut with a lightly oiled knife into small rectangles, about 2 x 4 cm.
